example.title: Cache a provider post for five minutes
description: Each tab names a file relative to the project root. Java `17` and Maven are required. `mvn spring-boot:run` starts this example after its external requirements are configured.
`PostApiClient.java`, the cache service, Redis settings, application class, and build file appear in these tabs.
The Spring Boot 3.5 project adds `org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-redis` with the Boot-managed version.
The web starter supplies Jackson and the managed `ObjectMapper`.
The Redis provider supplies the `REDIS_HOST`, `REDIS_PORT`, `REDIS_USERNAME`, and `REDIS_PASSWORD` environment values.
A caller invokes the injected `CachedPostService.read(1)` twice within five minutes.
A reachable Redis endpoint and provider are required.
explanation: Boot creates the connection and string template from the properties.
TLS certificate validation must remain enabled.
The key `post:v1:1` combines the record identity and a cache-format version.
On the first miss, `provider.read` retrieves the post.
`writeValueAsString` converts it to JSON before storage.
A later hit reads that JSON into the same response record.
No provider request occurs on that branch.
`set` supplies the value and expiry together.

richText: A cached value can remain old until expiry.
A source update can delete or replace its corresponding cache key sooner.
A Redis connection failure is different from a missing key.
An optional-cache policy can catch the relevant connection or decoding failures and use the original source.
A fallback needs recorded failures so a broken cache remains visible.
It must not hide failures from the original source.
Two simultaneous misses can both call the provider.
Expensive or rate-limited providers may need coordination.
String inputs in keys need a defined normalization rule.
Changing case is appropriate only when the underlying source treats those inputs as equivalent.
